name: Majestic Group Buy
shortDescription: Compare Majestic Group Buy access for backlink research. Explore referring domains, anchor text, Trust Flow and link history before choosing a plan.
description:
Majestic Group Buy is an option to compare when you need to study backlinks to a site or a particular page. A backlink is a link from another website to yours. A list of those links can help you see who refers to your work, which pages attract links and where a competitor has earned useful mentions. Start with one question and one site. A focused review is easier to act on than a large download with no context.

Majestic describes its tools as a way to explore links and linking sites. Look at the source page, the destination and the link text together. If you need a particular index, a report export or several searches in one session, ask whether the offer includes those features. Use the details for your own project when you compare access.

Start with a single page or a whole domain

A domain view gives you a broad picture of the links the tool has found across a website. That can help when you are preparing a first audit or comparing two sites in the same field. A page view gives you a closer look at one URL. It works well when you need to know why a particular guide or product page attracts references.

Choose the scope before you compare numbers. If you use one competitor’s entire domain and your own landing page, the results describe very different things. Use the same kind of search for both sides. Record whether the report covers an exact URL, a section or the domain, and note whether the URL you entered redirects to a different one.

Read the source page and the destination together

Look at a small set of results first. For each link, write down the page that contains it and the URL it points to. Open the source page if it is accessible. Read the sentence around the link to see why it was added. A reference from a local association may send interested readers even if it does not appear at the top of a metric sort.

Check the destination as well. A link can point to a helpful page, an old path that now redirects or a URL that returns an error. If a relevant site links to a missing resource, confirm whether you have a close replacement. The context of the original link helps you decide which replacement makes sense to the reader.

Understand referring domains and repeated links

A referring domain is a website that links to the site or URL you are studying. One domain can link many times. For example, a directory could repeat a link in the footer of hundreds of listings. A large backlink count can therefore come from a much smaller number of websites.

Review a few distinct domains before reading every backlink. Compare what kind of websites they are, what they say about the destination and whether the references are still visible. If many links appear in the same repeated placement, group them together in your notes. That helps you spend your time on links that add new information.

Read anchor text in context

Anchor text is the visible wording people click. A link could use your brand name, the title of your guide, the full URL or a phrase like “see the checklist.” The wording can tell you how another publisher describes the page, but the surrounding paragraph tells you why the link is there.

Sort or sample the anchors and look for patterns. If the same words appear many times, open some of the source pages to see whether they repeat a template. If a link looks odd, check the actual page and destination before drawing a conclusion. Include the context in your notes so someone else can understand what you saw.

Use Trust Flow and Citation Flow as starting points

Majestic offers its own metrics for exploring links. Trust Flow and Citation Flow can help you sort a list and choose examples to inspect. They are figures from Majestic’s own link data. The number alone does not tell you whether a link is helpful for a particular audience, whether a site is relevant or whether a page will rank.

Use the figures as one part of your review. If a site appears high on the list, open the linking page and check its purpose. If a useful industry resource appears lower, read it before setting it aside. A simple way to explain the results to a client is to show the source, the destination and why you consider the reference worth reviewing.

Compare a recent view with a longer look back

Majestic describes Fresh and Historic indexes. Confirm which index you can use with your offer and how it handles the period you want to study. A more recent view can help you explore links the tool has seen lately. A longer look back can give context when an old guide was moved or when you want to see references from earlier campaigns.

Record the index and the day you ran the report. An index is a record of what a crawler has observed. A missing result can mean a source was not seen in that view or the URL is different. When the link matters, open the source and destination in a browser before you decide whether it has been removed.

Find content that earns useful references

Pick a competitor that publishes for an audience similar to yours. Find a page with references from a few relevant websites. Look for the reason the references exist. The page may contain a free calculator, a reliable definition, a local resource or an example a writer can point readers to.

Use the pattern to plan your own resource. If an industry page links to a useful checklist, decide what your readers still need to know. A version with a specific example or a downloadable template could answer a different question. Write down the gap and make something you can keep accurate. The goal is to build a page people can refer to for a clear reason.

Review old links after a site move

If a site has moved or changed its URL structure, make a list of old pages that still have relevant links. Check where each old URL leads. An old guide about booking appointments should lead to a page that still helps a reader with booking, when a close match exists. Sending every old URL to a general page can make it difficult for visitors to find what they expected.

Record the highest priority problems and verify them yourself. Include the old URL, the current result and the proposed replacement. For links to an important page, check whether the source owner can update the reference after the destination is fixed. Keep the original report so you can repeat the checks after the change.

Compare Majestic with Ahrefs for your own workflow

If you searched for Majestic SEO and Ahrefs together, decide which question you want to answer first. Compare the tools on the same set of URLs. Record the dates and the scope. You may see different source lists because the tools collect and report links in different ways. Examine the overlap and review a few examples that appear in only one tool.

Try a small task such as checking links to a guide you recently moved. Compare how quickly you can find the source, confirm the destination and export the details you need. You can also review Ahrefs if your workflow combines link analysis with keyword research. Use the tool that gives you enough evidence for the decision at hand.

Check the access terms before you order

Ask which reports, indexes and search scopes are included. If you need a CSV or a report for a client, confirm that exports are available and what fields they include. Ask about the search allowance, whether limits reset and how access works on the browser you use. If you will be working on several projects, check how much work you can do in a normal session.

Compare the total cost of access with the work it lets you finish. A one-off review might only need a handful of URL searches. A monthly report could need repeated exports for several clients. If you are comparing group buy tools for several SEO tasks, see the group buy SEO tools catalog and check each product’s access details separately.

Frequently asked questions

Can Majestic show every backlink?

Each tool depends on the pages it crawls and the way it reports links. Use the results as a source of leads to review. For a critical link, inspect the source page directly and check whether the link goes to the destination you expect. When comparing two reports, note the index and date so the differences are easier to explain.

What should I check in an exported backlink report?

Look for a source URL, destination URL, anchor text and the dates or index fields you need. If you plan to share the file, add a column with your own review notes. A smaller set with verified examples can be easier for a teammate to use than a very large export with no explanation of what matters.

How do I decide which links to review first?

Start with links to pages that matter to your work. Then pick sources that appear relevant to the audience, links that point to a broken URL and examples that show a new pattern. Keep a short record of why you selected each one. This makes it easier to review changes on a repeat visit.

Can I use a Majestic score to judge a competitor?

Use the score to choose a starting point. Review the websites and pages behind it before deciding what the comparison means. A competitor with a popular free resource may earn different links from a competitor that mainly sells services. The source and purpose of the links can tell you more about the opportunity than the number alone.

How can I use this in a monthly client report?

Pick a few clear examples, explain why each matters and include the dates and report scope. Show the work you recommend next, such as repairing a page with useful incoming links or improving a resource that attracts references. Save your filters so your next review can use a comparable view.

Put the first review into practice

Choose a page you already know. Record its current URL and inspect a small set of backlinks. Group repeated domains, open the strongest examples and check where the links go. Turn the findings into a short action list with one owner for each task. An audit is more useful when the next person can see which links you checked and which pages need attention.

If you also need to turn audience questions into new pages, see AnswerThePublic. A link review can tell you why people refer to a resource, while search questions can help you decide what to explain next. Bring both findings into the brief and keep the evidence with the article so it can be reviewed later.

What would a useful backlink audit note look like?

Write the fact first, then the decision. For example, “The resources page of a local trade association links to our old appointment guide. The old URL returns an error. The updated appointment guide covers the same process, so it is a candidate replacement.” Include both URLs and when you checked them. Ask someone familiar with the site to review the proposed destination before they change anything.

You can use the same format when a link already works. “The association links to our checklist in a section about preparing for an inspection. The destination answers that question, so we can keep it as it is.” That second note matters because it distinguishes a link you reviewed from a link you did not open. Keep the findings short enough that someone can use them without having to read the entire export.

Review the relevance and context of referring domains alongside aggregate link metrics.
